title: Vectors, strings, maps
summary: The three collections you need: Vec, String, and HashMap.

blocks.html: A Vec is a list that grows. Every element has the same type, the elements sit next to each other in memory, and you can append to the end. It is the collection you will reach for first.

blocks.title: building and reading a Vec

blocks.html:
The vec! macro is shorthand for a new vector plus one push per element, and it tells the compiler the element type. There are two ways to read an element, and the difference matters:

  • v[0] checks the index at run time and panics when it is out of range.
  • v.get(0) returns Option<&T>: Some(&value) or None. The lesson on Option pays off here — nothing panics, and the compiler makes you say what happens when the index is empty.

pop returns an Option for the same reason: taking from an empty vector is not an error, it is just nothing.

To visit every element, loop over a reference. To change them, loop over a mutable reference.

blocks.title: get, then iterate by reference and by mutable reference
blocks.output:
Some(20)
None
index 9 is empty

[20, 40, 60]

blocks.title: a Vec is three words on the stack pointing at a heap buffer

blocks.html: String is a vector of bytes in a good coat: it owns its text, it can grow, and the bytes live on the heap. &str is a borrowed view into text someone else owns — a literal like "hello" is a &str baked into the program. Hold a String when you need to build text; ask for &str when you only need to read it.

blocks.title: growing a String
blocks.output:
Hello, world!
bytes: 13
Hello, world! I am Rust
Rust has 4 letters

blocks.html:
+ takes ownership of the left-hand side. That is why greeting cannot be used after the line that builds owned: it was moved into the result. The compiler says so plainly:

error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s`
note: calling this operator moves the left-hand side

Use format! instead. It borrows its arguments and returns a fresh String, so nothing is consumed and every input stays usable. Make format! the default and keep + for throwaway chains.

blocks.title: slicing with ranges, and walking chars

blocks.html:
A string slice is measured in bytes, not characters. "héllo" stores é in two bytes, so slicing &s[0..2] cuts a character in half and the program dies at run time with:

end byte index 2 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 1..3 of string)

When the text may contain non-ASCII characters, walk s.chars() instead of slicing, and remember that s.len() counts bytes while s.chars().count() counts characters.

blocks.title: counting words with a HashMap
blocks.output:
red: 3
blue: 1
black: never seen
black now: 9
distinct words: 4

blocks.html: Two facts to keep about HashMap. A missing key is not an error: get hands you an Option, exactly like Vec::get, while counts["red"] panics on a key that is not there. And the order you get from iterating is neither sorted nor the order you inserted — the map places keys wherever it likes. entry(key).or_insert(0) is the idiom to memorize: it returns a &mut to the existing value, or inserts the default and returns a reference to that, so *n += 1 writes through the reference and counts either way.

quiz.q: v holds three elements. What does v.get(9) do?
quiz.why: get returns Option<&T>, so an index outside the vector is None, not a panic. Only the square-bracket form v[9] panics.

quiz.q: Which line appends to an existing String without consuming it?
quiz.why: push_str borrows the string and appends in place. The + operator takes ownership of the left-hand side and moves it into the new value.

quiz.q: You insert red, blue, green into a HashMap and then iterate it. What order do you get?
options: Not sorted, and not the insertion order
quiz.why: A HashMap orders keys by their hash, which is effectively arbitrary and can change between runs. Sort the keys yourself when the order matters.

exercise.brief: Count the occurrences of every word. Start each unseen word at 0, then print one line per word in the form word count.
exercise.hint: counts.entry(w).or_insert(0) gives you a &mut i32: the current count if the word exists, or a freshly inserted 0 if it does not. Write through the reference with *n += 1.
